title: No NT word marks the image-ban ceremonial—unlike the Sabbath shadow in Colossians 2.16
source_text: XVI. Sed unde colligunt illi, praeceptum quo Deus prohibet ne imagines ullae colendae proponantur, positivum esse & ceremoniale? In quarto quidem praecepto aliquid esse ceremoniale, quatenus praecise Sabbatum, id est, septimum diem cujusque septimanae sanctificari jubet, colligimus ex Pauli Apostoli verbis disertis, Coloss. 2. 16. Ubi monet fideles non esse damnandos in cibo, vel in potu, aut in parte, seu distinctione diei festi, aut Neomeniae, aut Sabbatorum, quae omnia erant umbrae futurorum, quarum corpus in Christo est: sed ubi Christus, sive Apostoli tale quid significaverunt de prohibitione qua vetantur imagines ullae ad cultum fieri? Et num in toto Novo Testamento, vel unum verbum exstat, quo insinuetur Christianis licere Deum & Sanctos ejus in imaginibus colere, quod ante non licebat?
pass_a_gloss: But whence do they gather that the commandment by which God prohibits that any images be proposed to be cultivated is positive and ceremonial? In the fourth commandment indeed we gather that something is ceremonial, inasmuch as it precisely commands the Sabbath, that is, the seventh day of each week, to be sanctified, from the express words of the Apostle Paul, Coloss. 2. 16. Where he warns the faithful not to be condemned in food, or in drink, or in part, or distinction of a feast day, or of a New Moon, or of Sabbaths, which all were shadows of things to come, whose body is in Christ: but where have Christ, or the Apostles, signified any such thing concerning the prohibition by which any images are forbidden to be made for cult? And does there exist in the whole New Testament even one word by which it is insinuated that it is lawful for Christians to cultivate God and his Saints in images, which before was not lawful?
pass_b_english: Colossians 2.16 flags Sabbath/feast shadows as ceremonial; nothing parallel softens the image-ban.
The NT never whispers that Christians may now cult God or saints in images.
